summer.water: Check weekly. Water thoroughly when the orchid bark is nearly dry, then drain completely.
summer.feed: Use orchid fertiliser at the labelled dilution every third watering while new canes and roots are growing.

winter.water: Give a bright, cooler, drier rest. Water sparingly—just enough to prevent severe cane shrivelling.
winter.feed: Pause feeding during the winter rest; resume when active growth restarts.

care.meter: Not dependable in chunky orchid bark. Use pot weight, root colour and a wooden skewer instead.
care.light: Bright light is important for strong canes and flowering. Place close to a bright window, with protection from harsh midday sun, and monitor whether growth remains sturdy and it reblooms.
care.humidity: Moderate to high humidity with good air movement.
care.misting: Optional only where ventilation is good; avoid leaving flowers wet overnight.
care.temperature: About 18–25°C while growing; cooler nights help the winter rest, but protect from frost.
care.repotting: Repot only when the bark has broken down or the plant has outfilled its pot, ideally as new roots begin.
care.soil: Coarse, free-draining epiphytic orchid bark—not ordinary potting compost.
warningSigns: Soft black roots or sour bark suggest excess moisture
Cane shrivelling during active growth suggests insufficient water
Check for mealybugs and spider mites
care.notes: Do not remove firm old canes merely because they have flowered; they store energy and may flower again.

sources.label: RHS: Dendrobium nobile

summer.water: Check weekly; water when the top 2–3cm is dry. Drain fully and never leave it sitting in water.
summer.feed: Balanced liquid houseplant feed monthly at half strength during active growth.

winter.water: Check every 2–3 weeks and water when the upper compost has dried.
winter.feed: Pause, or feed very lightly every 6–8 weeks only if it is still actively growing.

care.meter: Water around 3–4/10, after the top few centimetres feel dry; avoid leaving it at 8–10.
care.light: Bright indirect light is ideal, although spider plants tolerate lower light. Protect from prolonged harsh direct sun.
care.humidity: Normal household humidity is usually adequate.
care.misting: Not required. Cleaning or showering the leaves occasionally is more useful.
care.temperature: Normal room temperatures; keep away from cold draughts and frost.
care.repotting: Repot every 1–2 years once the fleshy roots fill the pot.
care.soil: Peat-free multipurpose or houseplant compost with good drainage.
care.petSafety: Generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs, although chewing any plant may cause stomach upset.
warningSigns: Soft yellow growth suggests overwatering
Pale weak growth can indicate insufficient light
Brown tips can follow dry air, inconsistent watering or mineral-rich water
care.notes: Brown tips are common and can follow dry air, inconsistent watering or mineral-rich water; judge health from the plant’s overall vigour.

sources.label: RHS: How to grow spider plants

summer.water: Check every 5–7 days. Water when the top 2–3cm has dried, then let excess drain away.
summer.feed: Let it settle for 4–6 weeks, then feed monthly at half strength while actively growing.

winter.water: Check every 10–14 days; water only once the upper compost has dried.
winter.feed: Usually pause until spring unless it continues strong active growth.

care.meter: Water around 3–4/10, confirming the upper 2–3cm is dry; do not aim to keep it continuously moist.
care.light: Bright indirect or gently filtered light. Smaller leaves, long gaps between leaves or fading silver pattern suggest it needs more light.
care.humidity: Average household humidity is acceptable; moderate humidity supports better unfurling.
care.misting: Not necessary. Avoid keeping foliage persistently wet.
care.temperature: Warm and draught-free; ideally about 18–29°C.
care.repotting: Repot when roots are crowded or the mix drains poorly; avoid moving into a substantially oversized pot.
care.soil: Moisture-retentive but airy, free-draining houseplant mix.
care.petSafety: Toxic if chewed; contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals. Keep away from pets and children.
warningSigns: Yellow leaves can indicate excess water
Curling leaves can indicate thirst
Loss of silver pattern or stretched growth suggests insufficient light
care.notes: Judge establishment and suitability of a position from healthy new leaves rather than current fullness.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Scindapsus pictus

summer.water: Check every 3–5 days. Keep evenly moist, watering when the surface just begins to dry; never leave the pot waterlogged.
summer.feed: Feed monthly at half strength during active growth; pause after repotting or while the plant is acutely stressed.

winter.water: Check weekly and water before the rootball dries completely, while allowing free drainage.
winter.feed: Pause, or feed very lightly only if it remains in active growth.

care.meter: Aim to water around 4–5/10, before the root ball becomes fully dry; avoid sustained readings of 8–10.
care.light: Bright indirect light with no harsh direct sun. Sparse or weak new growth suggests it needs a brighter position.
care.humidity: Prefers high humidity. Measure humidity at leaf height to verify whether the humidifier makes a meaningful difference.
care.misting: Not a substitute for stable humidity. A humidifier and clean foliage are preferable to frequent leaf-wetting.
care.temperature: Warm, stable and draught-free; keep above about 15°C.
care.repotting: Repot when roots are crowded, ideally in spring, using a moisture-retentive but freely draining mix.
care.soil: Moisture-retentive but well-drained peat-free houseplant compost. Check the old central rootball as well as the fresh outer compost.
care.petSafety: Ctenanthe is generally regarded as non-toxic, but discourage chewing and seek veterinary advice if significant material is eaten.
warningSigns: Persistent tight curling can indicate moisture, root, humidity or pest stress
Fine pale stippling and webbing would support spider mites
A sour smell or soft dark roots would suggest excess moisture
Old damaged leaves will not repair—judge recovery by new leaves
care.notes: Persistent decline warrants checks for spider mites, water quality, root health and humidity rather than repeated preventative treatments.

summer.water: Check every 7–10 days. Water only when the upper 3–5cm is dry and a chopstick at root depth emerges nearly clean and only faintly damp; soak thoroughly and confirm that water drains freely.
summer.feed: Balanced liquid houseplant fertiliser monthly at half strength while actively growing.

winter.water: Check every 2–3 weeks and water sparingly once the upper compost has dried.
winter.feed: Pause until spring.

care.meter: Treat the meter as unreliable in this pot: it recently read about 10 while a chopstick indicated only slight moisture below a dry upper 4cm. Use chopstick moisture, pot weight and observed drainage together instead.
care.light: Bright indirect light with protection from direct sun; tolerates partial shade.
care.humidity: Moderate humidity. Measure at leaf height before deciding how much the humidifier helps.
care.misting: Optional and short-lived in effect; cleaning leaves and stable humidity are more useful.
care.temperature: Warm, sheltered conditions; avoid cold draughts and keep above about 15°C.
care.repotting: Repot infrequently and only when clearly root-bound; Kentias dislike unnecessary root disturbance.
care.soil: Free-draining peat-free loam-based palm or houseplant compost with added bark.
care.petSafety: Generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs.
warningSigns: Brown tips can follow dry air, mineral-rich water or inconsistent watering
Yellowing and soft roots suggest excess water
Check damaged foliage for scale, thrips and spider mites
care.notes: Kentia palms respond slowly. Change one care variable at a time and judge the result from new growth rather than old damaged fronds.

sources.label: RHS: Howea forsteriana

summer.water: Check every 4–7 days. Keep the compost evenly moist but never soggy; empty any standing water.
summer.feed: Balanced liquid palm or houseplant feed monthly at half strength.

winter.water: Check every 7–10 days; water when the surface begins to dry while keeping the rootball lightly moist.
winter.feed: Pause until active spring growth resumes.

care.meter: Water around 4–5/10; it prefers more even moisture than the Kentia but should not remain at 8–10.
care.light: Bright indirect light is ideal. Protect from prolonged direct sun, especially through hot glass.
care.humidity: Moderate to high humidity is preferred.
care.misting: Not essential; stable humidity and occasional leaf cleaning are more effective.
care.temperature: Warm room temperatures; protect from cold draughts.
care.repotting: Repot when root-bound into only a slightly larger pot; avoid breaking up the dense clump unnecessarily.
care.soil: Rich but free-draining houseplant or palm compost that remains lightly moist without becoming airless.
care.petSafety: Generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs.
warningSigns: Crisp tips can indicate dry air or uneven moisture
Yellow lower fronds can follow waterlogging
Inspect for spider mites and scale
care.notes: The identification is photo-based. Dense stemless basal clumping is the strongest distinguishing feature.

sources.label: Clemson Extension: Indoor palms
Kew: Chamaedorea cataractarum

summer.water: Check every 2–3 weeks and water thoroughly only after the compost has dried completely.
summer.feed: Cactus or succulent feed at half strength two or three times across spring and summer.

winter.water: Often every 4–6 weeks, but only when the compost is fully dry and leaves begin to soften slightly.
winter.feed: Do not feed.

care.meter: Wait for 1–2/10 in more than one spot before watering thoroughly; never keep it in the moist zone.
care.light: Very bright light to direct sun. Acclimatise gradually after a move from a dimmer position.
care.humidity: Normal dry household air is suitable.
care.misting: Do not mist routinely.
care.temperature: Normal room temperatures; keep frost-free and away from prolonged cold glass contact.
care.repotting: Repot only when crowded, using a pot with drainage holes; a heavy pot helps stabilise mature plants.
care.soil: Very free-draining cactus and succulent compost with added mineral grit.
care.petSafety: Potentially toxic to cats; keep out of reach if chewing is possible.
warningSigns: Soft translucent leaves or leaf drop suggest excess water
Wrinkled flexible leaves indicate thirst
Watch for mealybugs and scale
care.notes: An established plant that remains compact and unscorched can stay in its proven bright position.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Ripple Jade

summer.water: Check every 2–3 weeks and water thoroughly only after the compost has dried completely.
summer.feed: Cactus or succulent feed at half strength two or three times across spring and summer.

winter.water: Often every 4–6 weeks; water only when fully dry and the leaves begin to soften slightly.
winter.feed: Do not feed.

care.meter: Wait for 1–2/10 in more than one spot before watering; thick leaves store water between checks.
care.light: Bright light with some direct sun is ideal. Weak, stretched growth indicates insufficient light.
care.humidity: Normal dry household air is suitable.
care.misting: Do not mist routinely.
care.temperature: Average to cool room temperatures; keep frost-free.
care.repotting: Repot only when crowded into a slightly larger pot with reliable drainage.
care.soil: Very free-draining cactus and succulent compost with added mineral grit.
care.petSafety: Toxic to cats and dogs if eaten.
warningSigns: Soft translucent leaves or sudden leaf drop suggest excess water
Wrinkled flexible leaves indicate thirst
Watch for mealybugs, scale and spider mites
care.notes: Rotate occasionally if growth becomes strongly one-sided, but avoid frequent unnecessary moves.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Jade Plant

summer.water: Check every 2–3 weeks. Water only after the compost has dried fully, then drain completely.
summer.feed: Balanced liquid houseplant fertiliser once or twice across the growing season at half strength.

winter.water: Usually about monthly, and only if the compost is completely dry.
winter.feed: Do not feed.

care.meter: Wait for 1–2/10 at several depths and positions before watering; the mix can remain wet below a dry surface.
care.light: Tolerates low light but grows best in bright indirect light. Very low light slows growth and compost drying.
care.humidity: Normal household humidity is sufficient.
care.misting: Not required; wipe dust from leaves occasionally.
care.temperature: Ideally about 18–26°C; keep above 15°C.
care.repotting: Repot only once rhizomes crowd or distort the pot; use a pot only slightly larger.
care.soil: Free-draining houseplant mix amended for succulents; never leave the rhizomes wet.
care.petSafety: Toxic if chewed; contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
warningSigns: Yellow soft stems usually indicate excess water
Long weak growth may indicate insufficient light
Wrinkling can indicate prolonged drought
care.notes: Rapid new growth is positive, but increase watering only when the compost is actually dry.

sources.label: NC State Extension: ZZ Plant

summer.water: Water thoroughly only after the compost has dried completely—often every 2–3 weeks indoors.
summer.feed: One or two half-strength cactus-feed applications during spring and summer are sufficient.

winter.water: Water very sparingly, often every 4–6 weeks, only after complete drying.
winter.feed: Do not feed.

care.meter: Wait for 1–2/10 in more than one spot before soaking and draining; never keep the root zone continuously damp.
care.light: Very bright light with several hours of sun. Acclimatise gradually after any move to prevent scorch.
care.humidity: Low to normal household humidity.
care.misting: Do not mist routinely and keep water out of the central rosettes.
care.temperature: Warm and frost-free; avoid cold, wet compost.
care.repotting: Divide offsets or repot when severe crowding prevents watering, using a stable pot with several drainage holes.
care.soil: Very free-draining cactus and succulent compost with abundant mineral grit.
care.petSafety: Aloe vera can be toxic to cats and dogs if ingested.
warningSigns: Soft translucent bases suggest overwatering
Thin curling leaves can indicate prolonged drought
Watch for mealybugs and scale
care.notes: Use Aloe vera as the working identification, with species-level uncertainty retained.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Aloe vera

summer.water: Check daily in hot sunny weather. Keep evenly moist but not saturated; avoid repeated wilt-and-soak cycles.
summer.feed: Once flowering and fruiting, use a high-potassium tomato feed weekly at the labelled dilution.

winter.water: Usually grown as an annual. If overwintering indoors, reduce watering but do not let the rootball remain bone dry for long.
winter.feed: Pause during low-light overwintering.

care.meter: Water around 4–5/10 and keep moisture fairly even while flowering and fruiting; avoid repeated swings to 1 or sustained 8–10.
care.light: Full sun or the brightest available window; rotate periodically for even growth.
care.humidity: Normal household humidity with good airflow.
care.misting: Not required; avoid wetting flowers repeatedly.
care.temperature: Warm conditions; protect from temperatures below about 12°C and all frost.
care.repotting: Use a generously sized container with drainage if roots fill the current pot during active growth.
care.soil: Fertile, moisture-retentive but free-draining vegetable container compost.
care.petSafety: Fruit is edible when correctly identified, but foliage is not food. Cultivar and heat level are unknown.
warningSigns: Persistent wilt despite wet compost suggests root trouble
Blossom drop can follow heat or moisture stress
Inspect for aphids, whitefly and spider mites
care.notes: Indoor peppers need abundant light, warmth and regular feeding to sustain flowering and fruiting.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Capsicum annuum

summer.water: Check daily in warm sunny conditions. Keep moisture even and water thoroughly whenever the upper compost begins to dry.
summer.feed: Use tomato fertiliser weekly at the labelled dilution once the first fruits have set.

winter.water: Normally compost plants after the final harvest; tomatoes are generally treated as annuals in the UK.
winter.feed: No winter feeding unless deliberately maintaining a plant under strong supplemental light.

care.meter: Water around 4–5/10 while actively growing and fruiting; check daily in warm sun and avoid letting it swing from very dry to saturated.
care.light: As much direct sun as possible—ideally at least six hours. Indoor glass reduces useful light, so retain the brightest position.
care.humidity: Normal household humidity with strong airflow around the foliage.
care.misting: Do not mist routinely; dry foliage reduces disease pressure.
care.temperature: Warm growing conditions; protect from frost and very cold nights.
care.repotting: Use one large container per mature plant where possible, with secure support for indeterminate vines.
care.soil: Rich vegetable container compost with good drainage and consistent moisture.
care.petSafety: Ripe tomato fruit is edible; leaves, stems and unripe plant material should not be eaten by pets or people.
warningSigns: Uneven watering promotes fruit splitting and blossom-end rot
Excess nitrogen gives lush leaves but fewer fruit
Inspect for whitefly, aphids and spider mites
care.notes: Fruit colour alone is not enough to assign a cultivar; keep cultivar identification provisional unless labelled.

summer.water: Check every 7–10 days. Water thoroughly when the upper 3–5cm has dried, then drain completely.
summer.feed: Use a balanced liquid houseplant feed monthly at half strength while actively growing.

winter.water: Check every 2–3 weeks and water only after the upper compost has dried; low-light positions dry more slowly.
winter.feed: Pause until active growth resumes, unless strong growth continues under warm bright conditions.

care.meter: Water around 3/10 after confirming the upper compost is dry; never aim to keep the root zone continuously wet.
care.light: Bright indirect light is ideal. Protect from harsh direct sun; stretched growth or smaller leaves indicate insufficient light.
care.humidity: Average household humidity is acceptable, although moderate humidity supports larger, cleaner new leaves.
care.misting: Not required. Clean leaves and provide airflow rather than keeping foliage persistently wet.
care.temperature: Warm and draught-free; ideally about 18–27°C and above 15°C in winter.
care.repotting: Repot when roots are crowded or the mix has degraded, usually every 1–2 years for young plants.
care.soil: An airy, free-draining aroid mix with peat-free houseplant compost, fine bark and perlite or grit.
care.petSafety: Contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals and is toxic if chewed. Keep away from pets and children.
warningSigns: Yellow lower leaves and persistently wet compost suggest excess water
Long gaps between leaves suggest insufficient light
Check leaf joints and undersides for mealybugs, scale and spider mites
care.notes: Allow climbing species to use a support if larger mature foliage is wanted.
